etymologies.etymologyHTML: Inherited from Middle English cheep, chepe/chepen, chep, cheap/cheapien, chapien, from Old English cēap (“cattle, purchase, sale”), ċēapian (“to bargain, chaffer, trade”), from Proto-West Germanic *kaup (“trade, purchase”), *kaupōn (“to buy, trade”), from Proto-Germanic *kaupōną, *kaupijaną (“to buy, trade”), *kaupô (“inn-keeper, merchant”), from Latin caupō (“tradesman, innkeeper”). See also chapman. For sense evolution to "inexpensive," compare bargain or French bon marché.

quote.citation: c. 1597 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The First Part of Henry the Fourth, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene iii]:
quote.text: The sack that thou hast drunk me would have bought me lights as good cheap at the dearest chandler's in Europe.

definitions.definition: (Can we verify(+) this sense?) Cheapness; lowness of price; abundance of supply.

quote.citation: 1691, [John Locke], Some Considerations of the Consequences of the Lowering of Interest, and Raising the Value of Money. […], London:  […]  Awnsham and John Churchill, […], published 1692, →OCLC:
quote.text: Where there are many sellers and few purchases, land will be cheap.

quote.citation: 1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter III, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: One saint's day in mid-term a certain newly appointed suffragan-bishop came to the school chapel, and there preached on “The Inner Life.”  He at once secured attention by his informal method, and when presently the coughing of Jarvis  […]  interrupted the sermon, he altogether captivated his audience with a remark about cough lozenges being cheap and easily procurable.

quote.citation: 2000, George Abe, Residential Broadband, Cisco Systems, →ISBN:
quote.text: Datacasting bypasses the wired, terrestrial Internet and is a cheaper way to  distribute software than pressing and mailing CDs.

quote.citation: 2008, Amy Wechsler, The Mind-Beauty Connection, page 31:
quote.text: The cheapest antiager around: a good moisturizer.

quote.citation: 2013 July 20, “Out of the gloom”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8845:
quote.text: [Rural solar plant] schemes are of little help to industry or other heavy users of electricity. Nor is solar power yet as cheap as the grid. For all that, the rapid arrival of electric light to Indian villages is long overdue. When the national grid suffers its next huge outage, as it did in July 2012 when hundreds of millions were left in the dark, look for specks of light in the villages.

quote.citation: 1675, John Dryden, Aureng-zebe: A Tragedy. […], London:  […]  T[homas] N[ewcomb] for Henry Herringman, […], published 1676, →OCLC, (please specify the page number):
quote.text: You grow cheap in every subject's eye.

definitions.definition: (slang, of an action or tactic in a game of skill) Underhand or unfair.
(informal, chiefly derogatory) Stingy; mean; excessively frugal.
(finance) Trading at a price level which is low relative to historical trends, a similar asset, or (for derivatives) a theoretical value.
(computing) Taking little of system time or resources.
(intransitive) To trade; traffic; bargain; chaffer; ask the price of goods; cheapen goods.
(transitive) To bargain for; chaffer for; ask the price of; offer a price for; cheapen.

quote.citation: March 24 1658, John Milton, letter to Emeric Bigot
quote.text: I need not request you to purchase them as cheap as possible
